title: Four Non-Negotiable Teacher Mindsets
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart borrows the four academic mindsets from Camille Farrington's report and applies them to teachers: I belong in this professional community, my ability can improve with effort, I can succeed as a teacher, and this work matters. His blunt thesis is that a teacher who cannot affirm these must either change those beliefs or leave the profession, since without them teaching becomes painful and a career becomes a wasted life. He admits he lives in the first option, intellectually agreeing while sometimes acting as if one of the statements were false. He defines success as long-term student flourishing rather than test score movement, and warns against 70-hour weeks that make the work everything and eventually nothing. His closing implications for administrators urge building cultures that promote these mindsets, direct conversations rather than witch hunts, and extra attention to new teachers during transitions.
points: The four teacher mindsets, belonging, improvability, efficacy, and meaning, are framed as predictors of perseverance and effective practice.
Each mindset has a recognizable failure mode, such as isolation behind a closed door or reading the professional literature as optional.
Defining success as long-term student flourishing, not test scores, makes the efficacy mindset sane rather than grandiose.
Overwork and apathy both erode the belief that the work matters, so satisficing unimportant tasks and setting a work schedule are part of protecting it.
Leaders should shape cultures and have direct conversations, and should watch mindsets during transitions when they are most fragile.
quotes: Option A is where I live — repeatedly finding myself intellectually assenting to the four mindset statements that follow, but functionally, operationally working as if one or more of them aren’t true. Thinking as best we can is work.
And second, without these mindsets, teaching becomes painful, and sticking to it becomes an exercise in frustration. Such exercises, when they become entire careers, accumulate into the wasted life.

If you view yourself as having either no room for improvement (“I’ve arrived”) or no means through which to improve (“I am what I am; I’m just bad at X”), then you won’t improve. If you don’t believe that there’s more you can do or try in reaching That Student Who’s Failing or Those Kids Who Don’t Turn in Their Homework, your mind has no reason to work the problem and solve it.
First, you must define success sanely — not as simple test score movement, but as the promotion of the long-term flourishing of your kids. That is our single, enduring standard.

Others of you allow yourself to work 70 hours per week (and yes, it is working if you’re “relaxing” at night with a stack of student papers next to you), and so the work becomes everything and, eventually, nothing. (You need to set a work schedule.)
A kid we didn’t reach doesn’t mean the work didn’t matter. Teach long enough and you will inevitably hear from the kid you could’ve sworn you failed, only to find that you made an impact.

Teacher mindsets are probably most vulnerable at times of professional transition [4]. If a teacher enters a school and is led to believe that she doesn’t belong there or that she can’t improve or that she can’t succeed or that her efforts don’t matter, then her performance will suffer, and that suffering performance will reinforce her developing negative mindsets.
